item.title: Latest fraud scheme targets taxpayer-funded autism therapy boom
item.description: Medicaid paid over $5.15 billion for ABA therapy between 2018 and 2024, and prosecutors are now targeting alleged fraud schemes worth tens of millions.
item.content:encoded:
Applied Behavior Analysis therapy is a lifeline for hundreds of thousands of American families — helping children with autism develop communication, social and daily living skills.

But as Medicaid spending on the autism therapy has exploded into the billions and with fraud on the rise, a partisan divide is emerging over how states should handle public assistance programs for the ballooning treatment option.

Republican-led states like Florida have prioritized fraud enforcement and tighter oversight, while debates in states like Georgia have centered on reimbursement rates and preserving access to care. The scrutiny comes as the Trump administration has made it a focus of his second term to eliminate fraud, waste and abuse across federal programs, including Medicaid, a central policy priority.

Supporters of stronger oversight argue that every dollar lost to fraud is money that cannot be used to provide care for children and families who depend on Medicaid-funded autism therapy.

TRUMP ADMIN PAUSING OVER $1B IN MEDICAID PAYMENTS TO MINNESOTA, CALIFORNIA OVER FRAUD, COMPLIANCE CONCERNS

According to Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Medicaid provider spending data, Medicaid paid more than $5.15 billion between 2018 and 2024 under one of the primary billing codes used for Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) therapy.

Three providers received roughly $685 million in Medicaid reimbursements during that period.

ABA therapy is one of the most common treatments for children with autism, using structured, one-on-one sessions to build communication, social and daily living skills.

Much of that therapy is delivered by Registered Behavior Technicians (RBTs), entry-level workers who complete a 40-hour training program and work under the supervision of Board Certified Behavior Analysts, whose job it is to design and oversee treatment plans.

MEDICAID FRAUD FEARS GROW AMID MASSIVE RED STATE BILLING SPIKE IN SECTOR THAT ALSO PLAGUED MINNESOTA

As Medicaid spending on ABA therapy has surged, so has scrutiny over how taxpayer dollars are being spent.

In May, federal prosecutors charged two Minnesota autism clinic operators with allegedly billing Medicaid $46.6 million for services prosecutors say were unnecessary or never provided, including claims tied to children with allegedly fraudulent autism diagnoses.

Earlier this year, another Minnesota woman pleaded guilty in a separate $14 million Medicaid autism fraud scheme.

Investigations by The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times have also documented allegations that some providers billed for services that were never provided, inflated therapy hours and aggressively expanded as Medicaid spending surged.

MINNESOTA FRAUD SUSPECT SKIPS COURT, FORFEITS BOND, THROWING $11M MEDICAID CASE INTO DOUBT

The Medicaid data also identifies examples of providers receiving unusually large reimbursements under the ABA billing code, including some claims that equate to hundreds of dollars per minute of therapy based on a standard 15-minute billing unit. The data alone does not explain why those reimbursements were so high, and billing experts say unusually large payments can reflect a variety of factors, including claim adjustments or other administrative processes.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the federal agency that oversees Medicaid in partnership with states, told Fox News Digital it has observed "significant growth" in Medicaid spending on ABA therapy in recent years.

"While access to medically necessary services remains a priority, rapid program growth also underscores the importance of ensuring services are clinically appropriate, delivered by qualified providers, and supported by strong program integrity safeguards," a CMS spokesperson said.

As concerns over fraud have grown, states have responded differently.

Florida says it recovered more than $72 million in improper Medicaid payments over the past year and prevented hundreds of behavior analysts from participating in Medicaid because of documented fraud concerns.

Last month, Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis announced a statewide Medicaid Integrity Initiative to strengthen provider screening, enhance fraud detection and increase oversight aimed at protecting taxpayer dollars.

While Florida has focused on strengthening fraud enforcement, Georgia lawmakers have focused on reimbursement rates. Lawmakers recently questioned a Medicaid managed care organization's decision to reduce ABA reimbursement rates by 20%, even as industry representatives testified that use of autism therapy services had increased by more than 300% in recent years.

The debate reflects the difficult balance between rooting out fraud and preserving access to a therapy that many families say has been life-changing for children with autism.

item.title: Bryan Kohberger's choice of 'a house full of women' may hold the key to the Idaho murders' biggest mystery
item.description: The Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare" explores whether Bryan Kohberger's struggles with women fueled the deadly attack.
item.content:encoded:
Bryan Kohberger took the motive for the Idaho murders to his prison cell. One filmmaker believes the answer may lie in why he chose the house he attacked.

"The fact that [this] was the house that he chose. This was a house that had five women living in it. The night that the murders happened, Xana Kernodle’s boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, was over, but really, this was a house full of women, and it seems quite clear that he targeted it," Skye Borgman, director of the Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare," told Fox News Digital.

"He watched the house; he was around the house in the days, weeks and months leading up to the murders," Borgman said. "So, it seems pretty likely that he had a very low regard, if not hatred, for women."

IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

"It's all conjecture, but he seemed to struggle with his relationships with women," Borgman explained. "And we look at this incel movement and the question of whether or not he was an incel, and whether or not he didn't like women."

"It seems to me that there was a hatred of women there," Borgman added.

Kohberger, 31, is serving four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after pleading guilty to the 2022 stabbing murders of University of Idaho students Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen at an off-campus rental home in Moscow, Idaho.

Before his arrest, former classmate Lilly Karaban recalled him as someone with a "his way or the highway" attitude who seemed to exist "in his own world."

WATCH: KAYLEE GONCALVES’ MOTHER NOT SURPRISED BY KOHBERGER'S CLAIMS OF INNOCENCE, HOPES HE IS SENTENCED TO DEATH

Interviews, court records and accounts featured in the documentary described a series of troubling interactions involving Kohberger.

According to the documentary, classmates described him as "not particularly well liked," saying he frequently spoke down to women, engaged in "mansplaining" and became argumentative or aggressive during interactions. Several students said they found him "creepy" and that he made them feel uncomfortable.

"There were just strange incidents and strange behavior," Moscow Police Chief Anthony Dahlinger said in the documentary.

Former Washington State University Police Chief Gary Jenkins recalled another student's account of feeling cornered by Kohberger during an aggressive encounter. She also believed he occasionally followed her to her car. Kohberger was ultimately terminated from his teaching assistant position.

Jenkins said none of the reported incidents were referred to police because "nothing that occurred rose to the level of a crime."

Ed Jacobson, an FBI special agent involved in the investigation, said in the documentary that "we never saw evidence that shows Bryan Kohberger is part of the incel movement," an online community of mostly men who say they can't find romantic or sexual partners and often direct their frustration toward women.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"But Bryan Kohberger was very good at hiding his online activity," he noted.

For Borgman, the biggest question surrounding the Idaho murders remains the one Kohberger has never answered: why?

"I would love to, I think, along with the rest of the world, know why he did what he did," she told Fox News Digital. "But it is one of those things that I don't think any of us will ever know. That's a frustrating thing for myself ... and I know especially for the families. They wish so truly that he had been forced through the terms of his plea deal to give us more information about the why of it all."

In the documentary, Karaban said she believed Kohberger "has a thing against women based on the description of what he did to those poor three girls."

"People who brutalize women the way Kohberger did dislike them, find them threatening," she said. "So they take all that anger out on them."

Award-winning author James Patterson, who wrote a book on the case, previously told Fox News Digital his reporting uncovered multiple accounts of Kohberger engaging in unwanted interactions with women before his arrest.

SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER

At Seven Sirens Brewing Company in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, Kohberger would push his way into unwanted conversations with female bartenders and patrons. He went as far as asking for their addresses. Some women, according to the book, complained to the brewery's owner about "the creepy guy with the bulging eyes."

"Pretty much everybody we talked to just said, 'This is a strange man with a strange look — couldn't look people in the eye,'" Patterson said. "If he did look you in the eye, sometimes people wished that he hadn't. And his impression of himself was totally out of whack with the way other people perceived him."

In a police report obtained by Fox News Digital, an exotic dancer said a man she now believes was Kohberger visited the club where she worked in 2019, about two hours from his family's Pennsylvania home. She told investigators that while she was performing, the man remarked that he wanted to kill people. When she jokingly asked who, she said he replied, "Whoever I want."

Believing he was trying to get her attention, she alerted bouncers to keep an eye on him. She said the encounter didn't stand out again until she saw Kohberger's photo on television after his arrest and became fairly certain he was the man she had encountered.

Borgman believes Kohberger was trying "to commit the perfect crime."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"He failed in doing that," she said. "But I think his silence is a way of attempting to keep the spotlight focused on him."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Borgman said police are also "grappling with the why."

"We spoke to one of the FBI agents who worked the case, and he essentially says, 'You've got to be OK with not knowing,'" Borgman said. "And that's really hard for humans to do: be OK with not knowing. And to crawl inside somebody's mind and figure out the whys ... it's impossible. And I think that's one of the reasons people followed this case for so long. ... That question of the why still lingers with just about everybody."

SEND US A TIP

After years of searching for answers, the victims' families are no longer waiting for them, Borgman said. Instead, they're focused on honoring their loved ones' legacies.

"I don't think they expect the perpetrator to talk," she said. " ... The families now are looking forward, not backward. ... Every one of them is committed to trying to help families who may be going through something like this."

"So while I don't want to say they're hopeful, every one of them is taking this tragedy and trying to make something good out of it because that's the only thing they can do," she said. "They can't carry around the hatred in their lives, or else it'll just consume them. So they carry the love forward. And the love is really with Ethan, Maddie, Kaylee and Xana."

Just two days before the documentary premiered on July 29, Kohberger made a dramatic bid to withdraw his guilty plea. He asked a judge to let him stand trial instead, alleging his attorneys pressured him into accepting a plea deal by promising better prison conditions and warning him about life on death row.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

In his request, Kohberger said his attorneys didn't adequately represent him and that his guilty plea wasn't knowingly or voluntarily entered because it "was induced by unkept promises" and threats, The Associated Press reported.

In 2025, Kohberger said he was pleading guilty "freely and voluntarily." In doing so, he agreed to waive his rights to appeal, confirm that he understood the penalties for the crimes and assure the court that he wasn't coerced by his attorneys or anyone else to enter the plea. In exchange, prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty.

Borgman said some investigators involved with the case were so shaken by the crime and its impact on Moscow that "they don't work in law enforcement anymore."

"It's something that was too much, and they ended up leaving the police force," she said. "So it's important, I think, to really factor into what happened, the incredible toll it takes on law enforcement and the incredible toll it takes on the community."

"So many people felt fear," she said. "The fear was so deep that they weren't leaving their homes. And that fear, along with the arrest of the perpetrator, also led to this amazing feeling of community. It brought people together."

item.title: Paidwork breach exposes 23M user records
item.description: The Paidwork data breach exposed 23 million accounts including bank account numbers, addresses and password hashes from the microtask platform.
item.content:encoded:
Making a few extra dollars online should not put your bank details or identity at risk. Yet that is the concern for people who used Paidwork, an online earnings application.

A leaked database tied to the platform reportedly contains information from more than 23 million accounts. If you ever signed up, now is a good time to take the warning seriously.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

COULD THE 7-ELEVEN BREACH AFFECT YOU?

Paidwork is a microtask platform that offers small payments for completing online activities. Those jobs can include answering surveys, testing apps and watching advertisements. You complete tasks, build a balance and eventually request a payout. For many people, the account may feel low risk because the earnings are small. However, the information behind those payments can be far more valuable.

Hackers claimed in March 2026 that they had obtained data from Paidwork. They later offered the information for sale. Nearly 11 GB of data allegedly taken from the platform appeared publicly in July. The data breach notification service Have I Been Pwned analyzed the released files and found more than 23 million unique email addresses. The service added the incident to its database on July 19, 2026.

Paidwork told CyberGuy it is actively investigating the reported breach, working with external security specialists and taking steps to protect affected accounts and notify users as appropriate.

The exposed information appears to reach far beyond email addresses. Have I Been Pwned says the files contain names, phone numbers, physical addresses and dates of birth. They also reportedly include education levels, gender information, profile photos and personal interests.

The financial records raise additional concern. The files reportedly contain bank account numbers, transaction information and payout histories. Attackers may also have device information and IP addresses. Those details can reveal how you connected to the service and which equipment you used.

Finally, the leak reportedly contains passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. Bcrypt makes passwords harder to crack than weaker storage methods. However, short or predictable passwords can still face attacks. That is a huge amount of personal information to exchange for tasks that may pay only a few cents.

WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

You may have earned very little through Paidwork. A criminal could still find plenty of value in your account. For example, a phishing email could mention a real payout before claiming that your bank transfer failed. Another message could include your address to make a fake security warning look convincing.

Criminals can combine several leaked details to build a believable story around you. Password reuse creates another danger. If attackers crack your Paidwork password, they can test it on other websites. This type of attack is called credential stuffing. It succeeds when people reuse one password across several accounts. Your email account should cause the greatest concern. Someone who gets inside may use it to reset passwords for other services.

Bank account numbers and transaction histories can also support convincing fraud attempts. A caller who knows your payment history may sound like a legitimate representative. Attackers do not care how much you earned. They care how much they can make from the information connected to you.

This leak should make all of us think carefully about the information we give side-income platforms. A task may pay only a few cents. Meanwhile, the service may request your legal name and bank account information before releasing your earnings.

It may also collect your birth date, home address or information about your device. That creates an uneven trade. Before joining an earning app, review what information it collects. Look for an explanation of why the company needs each detail.

Also, check whether you can delete your account after you stop using the platform. Find out whether you can remove old payout methods and profile information. Avoid completing optional profile fields that reveal extra details about your life. The company cannot lose information that you never provided. You should also think carefully before connecting your primary bank account to a service you plan to use only occasionally.

Have I Been Pwned lists the Paidwork incident as affecting 23.3 million accounts. You can search the email address you used for the platform through its breach-checking tool.

A match means your email address appears in the released files. However, the public search will not display every exposed detail connected to you. You should still secure your accounts when a search produces no match. Public breach databases may contain incomplete records.

Also, make sure you visit the real Have I Been Pwned website. Criminals often create fake breach-checking pages to collect more personal information. Never enter a password, Social Security number or banking information into a breach-search tool.

Start with your login credentials and financial accounts. Then reduce the amount of personal information criminals can find elsewhere.

To see if your email was affected, visit Have I Been Pwned at haveibeenpwned.com . It is the first and official source for this newly added dataset. Enter your email address to find out if your information appears in the Synthient leak. When done, come back here for Step 2.

Change the password connected to your Paidwork account, even if you no longer use the platform. Create a completely new password. Avoid adding a symbol or number to your old password because criminals often test common variations. Next, change that password on every other account where you reused it. Also, immediately replace an exposed password anywhere you used it.

A password manager can create and store a different password for each account. That limits the damage from one exposed login. You also avoid relying on short passwords that are easier to remember and crack. Protect the password manager with a strong master password. Then enable multifactor authentication for the password manager itself.

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) anywhere the option appears. Start with your email account. Then protect your bank, payment services and other important accounts. An authenticator app or security key usually provides stronger protection than a text message. However, any second verification step can improve your security.

Contact any bank or payment service you connected to Paidwork. Explain that your account information may appear in a leaked database. Ask whether the institution recommends extra monitoring or a replacement account number. Next, turn on alerts for withdrawals and transfers. You should also receive a warning when someone changes your account information. Report any transaction that you do not recognize. Do not ignore a small charge because criminals sometimes use minor transactions to test an account.

A credit freeze can help stop someone from opening a new credit account in your name. You need to place the freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze costs nothing to place or remove. You do not need to wait for evidence of identity theft. The FTC says a credit freeze can help after your personal information appears in a data breach. Remember that a credit freeze cannot prevent fraud involving an account you already have. Continue watching your existing bank and credit card statements.

Be suspicious of emails, texts or calls that mention Paidwork, a payout or a bank transfer. A criminal may know your full name or address. That knowledge does not prove the message came from a legitimate company. Avoid clicking links in unexpected messages. Open the official app or type the company's address into your browser instead. Never share a verification code with someone who contacts you. Criminals often request those codes while trying to enter your account. Phishing links can steal information or install malware on your device.

Strong antivirus software can warn you about malicious links, infected attachments and fake websites. This protection becomes especially useful after a breach. Criminals often send fake security alerts that pressure you to download a file or visit a login page. Keep your security software updated so it can recognize newer threats. However, antivirus protection cannot catch every convincing scam. Continue checking the sender and web address before clicking anything. The FTC recommends using security software to protect your devices from malware and other online threats. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

The Paidwork files reportedly contain information that may also appear on people-search websites. A data removal service can send opt-out requests to data brokers that collect and sell personal information. Reducing those records may make it harder for criminals to expand a leaked profile. You can also submit the removal requests yourself for free. However, you may need to contact many sites and repeat the process when your information returns. A data removal service cannot erase the Paidwork files from criminal forums. It also cannot remove government records or every old listing from the internet. The FTC says people-search sites usually provide an opt-out process. It also notes that paid services can complete requests on your behalf. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

A platform may pay you a few cents while storing information that can affect your life for years. The Paidwork files reportedly combine personal profiles with banking information and password hashes. That gives criminals several ways to target you, even when your Paidwork balance was nearly empty. Paidwork says it has no confirmed evidence its systems or accounts were compromised. However, Have I Been Pwned found more than 23 million unique email addresses in the publicly released files. Treat the warning seriously if you ever used the platform. Change reused passwords first. Then secure your financial accounts and watch for messages that know a little too much about you.

How much personal information should a side-hustle platform be allowed to collect for a few dollars in return? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Kamala Harris backs major changes to the Supreme Court, Electoral College ahead of possible 2028 campaign
item.description: Former Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed Supreme Court expansion and abolishing the Electoral College at the National Urban League Conference while weighing a 2028 run.
item.content:encoded:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Friday embraced a series of progressive policy proposals she did not campaign on in 2024, including expanding the Supreme Court and abolishing the Electoral College, as she continues weighing a potential 2028 presidential bid.

Speaking at the National Urban League Conference in Nashville, Tenn., Harris endorsed several proposals she did not publicly campaign on during her 2024 White House run.

"We must allow for a real conversation about revisiting certain things," Harris said. "I know this is gonna be controversial coming from me, in particular. We need to revisit the Electoral College."

HILLARY CLINTON STILL FUMING OVER ELECTORAL COLLEGE, CALLS IT AN 'ABOMINATION' IN NEW NETFLIX SERIES

Harris lost both the Electoral College and the popular vote to President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.

She also voiced support for expanding the Supreme Court.

"We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts," Harris said.

SEN DEB FISCHER: THE LEFT'S WAR ON THE SENATE AND SUPREME COURT PUTS OUR REPUBLIC AT RISK

While Harris has previously supported term limits for Supreme Court justices, expanding the court was not part of her 2024 campaign platform.

She also suggested the U.S. should revisit statehood for Puerto Rico, expanding beyond her previous support for statehood for Washington, D.C.

Despite the new policy positions, Harris said she has not yet decided whether she will seek the presidency in 2028.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

"I have not made a decision," she told attendees. "I am fully, sincerely, focused on these midterms."

Harris' remarks come as multiple Democratic aides and strategists have suggested she is the leading contender for the party's 2028 presidential nomination.

When asked by Rev. Al Sharpton at the National Action Network's 35th Anniversary Convention in April whether she planned to run for president again, Harris left the door open.

"I might. I might. I'm thinking about it... I'll keep you posted," she said.

Harris' comments also come after she has recently courted progressive Democrats, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Fox News Digital previously reported that Harris called Mamdani in May and later met privately with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., during a Black women's empowerment summit in Chicago.

The outreach comes as Harris continues meeting with influential figures on the Democratic Party's progressive wing ahead of a possible 2028 campaign.

Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser, Hannah Brennan and Andrew Mark Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: Nancy Guthrie sheriff says investigators may have more video evidence as they review thousands of clips
item.description: Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos says he believes there's more video evidence as investigators comb through 'tens of thousands' of clips. Ransom notes released in bid to ID suspect.
item.content:encoded:
TUCSON, Ariz. — The sheriff overseeing the investigation into the suspected abduction of Nancy Guthrie has released two purported notes that may have been sent by one of her kidnappers as he urged anyone with information to come forward and appeared confident that investigators remain on the right track — revealing that investigators are reviewing "tens of thousands" of videos.

Saturday marks six months since the 84-year-old mother of "Today" co-host Savannah Guthrie was taken from her longtime home in the Catalina Foothills on Feb. 1. 

Savannah Guthrie on Saturday shared an emotional Instagram post marking six months since her mother was abducted, saying her family has "lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair" while pleading for anyone with information to come forward. "We will never stop looking for answers," Guthrie wrote, urging anyone who knows something to contact investigators anonymously and help "bring her home."

While there have been no arrests in the case and no suspects have been publicly identified, Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos told Fox News Digital he's optimistic that investigators will crack the case.

NANCY GUTHRIE'S SUSPECTED ABDUCTION: TIMELINE OF EVENTS IN DISAPPEARANCE OF 'TODAY' HOST'S MOM

"We're not even close to these leads being dried up," he said. "We'll continue to work them, and even if they all dried up and we had nothing else to go on, we have a cold case unit."

In a wide-ranging interview Thursday, the sheriff discussed new developments in the investigation, setbacks, cooperation with the FBI and why he believes the case will be solved.

Here are six key takeaways:

Task force members are still going through a large number of video and may have more images of the suspect, the sheriff said.

"We have so many thousands of pieces of video, literally tens of thousands, that what happens daily is the team looks at these videos and really they're just kind of compartmentalizing them," Nanos told Fox News Digital.

Investigators are still examining the video for clues and sorting them in a way that they can be quickly reassessed later if new context or evidence emerges, he said.

NANCY GUTHRIE UPDATE: DNA COULDN'T BE PROFILED FROM CRIME SCENE HAIR SAMPLE, SHERIFF SAYS

"We take them and, hey — here's a red car. Give me all the red cars; let's compartmentalize them," he said.

That's done because down the line, someone may get arrested in a red car similar to one that police can already place near the crime scene.

"Now we can go back to those videos and say, 'Aha — this is the same red car,'" Nanos said. "That kind of thinking."

He declined to discuss specific evidence, but investigators have previously been seen canvassing the surrounding neighborhoods, major intersections and commercial areas for video that could help in the case. The FBI also removed home security cameras from Guthrie's roof and backyard back in February.

Months after Google and the FBI teamed up for the groundbreaking recovery of Nest doorbell video that shows the only known images of a suspect in the case, Nanos said other major companies around the country are also helping out.

"It may be Google today, it could be, I don't know, pick another large company that says, 'Hey, sheriff, you know, we work at this and I think we might have something that can help there," he said.

Google, which helped recover cached imagery from a backend system, is just one example, he said.

"Google comes up because they were the ones that first came out with the development of that one photo that was released. And it was critical, right? This is who we believe is the guy. It's the only piece of evidence we have that says, here's a picture of him right now. Does that mean other evidence doesn't exist, video or otherwise? No, I think it does. I think it's out there. And maybe we have some of that."

The sheriff said companies have been reaching out with specialized technology and expertise that may help investigators.

"So I like to think that we have some of the best minds in the nation, if not the world, that are trying to solve this case," he said.

Nanos has downplayed suggestions of meaningful friction between his office and the FBI during the investigation, telling Fox News Digital the detectives and FBI agents on the case are working together on a Guthrie task force assembled from members of the long-standing Southern Arizona Violent Crime Task Force.

"You have the videos of those first days of press conferences," he said. "Who's standing there with the sheriff? I mean, it's like right after we get done with the crime scenes, we come out, day one or two, whatever it is, there's a press conference. In fact, in the first four days, there's two press conferences. And who's on the stage with the sheriff? Not just the FBI special agent in charge of Tucson, but the special agent and in charge of all of Arizona."

Additionally, he said local members of the FBI's violent crimes task force were called to the scene on day one and described a close, ongoing working relationship between sheriff's detectives and the FBI, with daily coordination between the agencies.

"My team that is assigned to the FBI office here locally, they meet every day with the FBI, with their managers, with my supervisors and command staff," Nanos said.

He said local members of the FBI's joint task force have been part of the case since "day one" and remain involved six months later.

Investigators couldn't obtain a DNA profile from a hair sample recovered inside Nancy Guthrie’s home, Nanos said, but rapid advances in technology mean other evidence could yield new leads. And the hair itself could still be used to compare to a suspect if one is ever identified.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"It came back ... there's no DNA," Nanos said. "But does that mean the hair isn't that of the suspect? We won't know that till we have the suspect's hair. You don't just destroy it."

Nanos indicated the hair was only one part of the broader DNA work underway, though he did not specify how many other samples are being tested. Fox News Digital has previously reported that there was also a mixed sample collected from the home, and sources said early on that a cutting from Guthrie's bedding had also been sent to a crime lab.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"Anything we can grasp onto with DNA is a part of this investigation," he said.

That includes investigative genetic genealogy research, which is used to generate leads from a family tree.

New evidence could quickly turn the focus of investigators back to people who have been previously cleared, the sheriff said.

NANCY GUTHRIE CASE: SHERIFF SAYS NO ONE IS PERMANENTLY RULED OUT AS DETAINED MAN PREPARES LAWSUIT

"From what we have in front of us, the evidence, the DNA, the whatever, the videos. Yeah, I think you can eliminate them," Nanos told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview Thursday. "And so that elimination happens. But it's like any [criminal case], because you're eliminated doesn't mean you didn't do it. It doesn't mean that we can't get more information."

New evidence could put anyone back in the investigation’s focus, Nanos said.

"I think I early on said, 'Look, there is no suspects. The family is not suspects. They’re not," he told Fox News Digital. "Now, does that mean that ends it forever? No. What happens if next week somebody calls and says, ‘Hey, a family member did this, and here’s how I know it’? You know that always opens a door."

GOT A TIP?

Investigators believe someone may be able to help identify the masked man seen in Guthrie's Nest doorbell video.

"We believe, just as the family does, just as Savannah does, somebody knows something," Nanos said. "We need that person to call us."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

His office also released a pair of notes that may have been sent by one of Guthrie's abductors. While authorities haven't yet confirmed the notes are legitimate — they haven't ruled them out either. And Guthrie's daughter, Savannah Guthrie, has said she believes they may be real.

The sheriff's department said the notes share a "unique linguistic style" and could have been written by the same person. Investigators are asking for the public's help identifying that person.

"As with the unidentified male depicted in the video, we believe these distinctive linguistic characteristics may be recognizable to someone who knows or has interacted with the notes' writer," authorities said. "A friend, family member, coworker, classmate, or acquaintance may recognize these patterns of expression and possess information that could help identify the individual responsible."

Anyone with information is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI or, to remain anonymous, call 520-88-CRIME.

The sum of all rewards in the case is over $1.2 million — none of which has been claimed.

item.title: 100 days until midterms and Democrats are winning because they actually have a message
item.description: Democrats have unified their midterms message around affordability while Republicans offer a menu of issues without a single organizing story.
item.content:encoded:
With 100 days until the midterms, one thing has become surprisingly clear.

Democrats know exactly what election they want to run.

Republicans still don’t.

100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY

I’m not talking about policy. Republicans have plenty of issues that resonate with voters.

I’m talking about something much simpler.

The story.

LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN

After three decades studying how people make decisions, I’ve learned that people don’t vote issue by issue. They don’t carry around a mental spreadsheet comparing tax policy, border security, energy production and education reform.

They simplify.

They look for one idea that helps them make sense of everything else.

THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH

That’s what Democrats have done.

They’ve taken a complicated election and reduced it to one word:

Affordability.

Whether or not you agree with their solutions isn’t the point. From a communications perspective, they’ve done something incredibly powerful: they’ve given voters a lens.

Every new headline about rising costs reinforces the same story.

That’s what great messaging does. It doesn’t just communicate. It organizes.

Republicans, meanwhile, have no shortage of winning issues.

Immigration.

Those are all important conversations. Many poll extremely well.

But they’re still individual conversations.

Collectively, they don’t tell one story.

That’s the difference between having a message and having a menu.

One gives people clarity.

The other gives them choices.

As someone who studies persuasion, I can tell you that clarity almost always wins.

Republicans’ closest thing to a national message is that Democrats have become too extreme. That they’re too far left, too ideological, too willing to let government expand into every part of American life.

That message energizes Republicans. It persuades some independents, too.

But notice where it starts.

It starts with Democrats.

Affordability starts with voters.

That’s a fundamental difference.

Most Americans aren’t waking up asking whether Washington has embraced democratic socialism.

They’re asking why groceries still cost so much.

They’re wondering why buying a home feels out of reach.

They’re looking at insurance bills, child care costs and monthly budgets.

Democrats have decided that every road leads back to that conversation.

Republicans are still asking voters to connect the dots across half a dozen different conversations.

That may be enough.

It may not.

But with only 100 days left, the biggest advantage Democrats have isn’t necessarily on the issues.

It’s that they’ve decided what the election is about.

Republicans haven’t.

And in politics, the party that defines the election usually starts with the upper hand.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The next 100 days won’t simply determine who wins the House or Senate. They’ll determine which story voters carry with them into the voting booth.

Because elections are rarely won by the party with the longest list of arguments.

They’re won by the party that gives people the simplest way to understand the moment they’re living through.
